UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE, Plaintiff, v. KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6, Defendants. ____________________________________/ | Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

PLAINTIFF’S REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION FOR REFERRAL TO AN EARLY SETTLEMENT CONFERENCE

Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited Children and Katie Hall acknowledge the Court’s authority to order a settlement conference under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(a)(5). ECF No. 136 at 2. They identify no legal prohibition against the requested referral. Instead, they characterize Plaintiff’s interest in conciliation as insincere, describe his proposed amendment as harassment, and attribute the volume of proceedings exclusively to him. Id.

The record supplies relevant context that their opposition omits.

On July 31, 2026, at the beginning of this action, Plaintiff transmitted a proposed settlement agreement offering to release the claims against NCMEC and Hall without requiring either defendant to pay any money or admit any wrongdoing. Plaintiff would bear the deposition recording costs. In exchange, Hall and NCMEC would provide sworn testimony concerning the April 22 letters, together with limited document production. Upon performance of the agreement’s conditions, Plaintiff would release the covered claims.

The agreement did not require testimony favorable to Plaintiff. Section 2.5 expressly disclaimed any requirement that either witness corroborate Plaintiff’s allegations or provide a particular answer. Section 7.2 likewise made completion independent of whether testimony favored Plaintiff, established wrongdoing, or produced any particular litigation result.

Those provisions were consequential. Plaintiff did not know what the underlying CyberTipline records contained. The proposed depositions could have supplied evidence undermining his claims, corroborating NCMEC’s position, or otherwise materially adverse to his interests. Plaintiff offered the release notwithstanding that possibility.

The agreement therefore offered no guaranteed vindication. It offered a defined means of obtaining sworn evidence and concluding the claims against NCMEC and Hall, without payment or admission. The parties could have begun that resolution process in August. NCMEC did not accept the proposal.

NCMEC now asserts that Plaintiff’s interest in conciliation rings hollow and that Plaintiff alone caused the volume of proceedings. ECF No. 136 at 2. But the July 31 proposal demonstrates that Plaintiff offered an earlier means of resolving the claims through testimony that was not required to favor him. Its rejection did not establish that the underlying claims were frivolous or that Plaintiff’s purpose was harassment.

Plaintiff identifies this settlement history for the limited purpose of informing the Court’s assessment of the proposed referral and NCMEC’s resource-efficiency objection, not to prove liability, establish damages, or impeach by contradiction. Fed. R. Evid. 408(a)–(b).

The distinction between settlement and the underlying factual dispute remains important. NCMEC has defended the April 22 letters as true while maintaining that Plaintiff cannot plausibly contest their truth because he lacks access to the reports. ECF No. 11 at 8–9. Nothing in ECF No. 136 establishes whether any CyberTipline report, as originally received, contained or otherwise identified Plaintiff’s complete legal name, “Marvelle J. Ballentine.” That factual issue remains the subject of Plaintiff’s separate efforts to obtain limited discovery.

NCMEC is entitled to decline settlement. Plaintiff does not request an order compelling NCMEC or Hall to accept an agreement or make concessions. Plaintiff likewise does not contend that declining settlement establishes liability.

The Court may evaluate the utility of a referral under Rule 16 without adopting NCMEC’s unsupported characterizations of Plaintiff’s motives. Plaintiff submits the foregoing in reply to the opposition and maintains the request presented in ECF No. 133.

Marvelle J. Ballentine
